progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From B11: a SNP is a one-base difference, each version an allele; reading both copies gives the genotype; allele frequency = copies / all copies; association is not cause. From B9: pedigree symbols; unaffected parents with an affected child show a recessive trait; carriers. From B7: the sickle allele is one base change, GAG to GTG on the coding strand. From B5b and B8: each parent passes one copy of each chromosome; genes on different chromosomes are inherited independently. From B4: bases A, T, C, G and complementary pairing. From B6a: DNA is packed into chromosomes. Not assumed: sequencing, profiling, short tandem repeat, gel electrophoresis, band, match probability.
progression.startsWith: A specified research question needs sequencing or profiling evidence. The video opens: In 1985, British officials doubted that a boy returning from Ghana was really his mother's son. A geneticist, Alec Jeffreys, had just found a way to compare people's DNA as patterns of bands.
progression.stopsAfter: saying that sequencing determines the exact order of bases in a stretch of DNA and profiling compares a few selected variable markers without reading the order; describing sequencing as reading short copied fragments base by base and assembling them by overlap; using sequencing to find a single-base variant directly, including carriers (two bases at one position), and to give allele frequencies across a population; describing a short tandem repeat as a short sequence repeated side by side, with repeat numbers that vary, two copies per person (one from each parent); explaining that DNA moves to the positive electrode because it is negatively charged and shorter fragments travel further; using "every child band comes from the mother or the father" to identify paternal bands and exclude a man; explaining why a match needs many independently inherited markers (chances multiply) and is not proof; choosing sequencing for a question about a particular base and profiling for relatedness or identity, with the limits of each; applying this to an unseen paternity gel and an unseen tool-choice question.
progression.nextLesson: what large collaborative population-genetics projects can show (route entry bio-m5-b13).

teaching.task: How can DNA itself show who inherited what, and when should you read every base rather than compare a few markers?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why sequencing needs assembly (it reads short fragments, 3); why carriers show two letters (two copies read together, 4); why repeat lengths differ between people (repeat number varies, 5); why DNA moves and why short pieces move further (negative charge; easier passage through the gel, 6); why every child band matches a parent (one copy from each, 7); why a match is weaker than a mismatch (shared patterns; chances multiply only for independently inherited markers, 8); why profiling can't find a disease allele (it measures lengths, mostly in non-coding DNA, 9). Visible case: one family trace, one trio gel, one ladder, one choice board. Video advantage: fragments snap together by overlap; double peaks appear on carriers; bands race and settle; joining lines show which parent gave each band; the ladder multiplies live. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items with every band and demand on screen. Reading load: one board at a time; the attempt 1 card (three gels, four lanes each) is the densest frame and is the task itself.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Conversational, one board at a time, causes before names. Scene 2 says what each tool measures before naming either one. Scene 5 shows the repeated unit and the different repeat counts before naming "short tandem repeats". Scene 6 explains why DNA moves and why short pieces move further before naming the band. Scene 8 shows why chances multiply before saying "many markers". Analogy: One, small and true to the mechanism: assembling overlapping fragments is like matching the edges of torn strips (scene 3), because both work only where pieces share an overlap. The contrast "one reads every letter; the other checks a handful of markers" (scene 2) is literal, not an analogy.
teaching.openingDecision: So how can a pattern of bands show who's related? And how is that different from reading DNA one base at a time?
teaching.understandingCheck: 11a is a paternity gel at three markers (mother, child, man A, man B; one man excluded at two markers, the other consistent at all three): it tests the "child band from mother or father" rule, identifying the paternal band first, exclusion and the limit of inclusion. 11c is the site's tool-choice question (a disease-linked single-base variant in two populations) with a second demand to name a question where profiling is better: it tests what each tool measures. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; each card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reason, short working on the card, one crossed-out classic mistake. No mark-allocation talk.
teaching.curriculumScope: "investigate the use of technologies to determine inheritance patterns in a population using, for example: (ACSBL064, ACSBL085)" with the example "DNA sequencing and profiling (ACSBL086)". Route action B-technologies (ledger row p1068). The parent line is marked as a depth-study or practical opportunity in the syllabus JSON; this video supplies the concepts and two analysis tasks, not a student investigation. Update ledger row p1068 when this design passes review.

design.visualSystem: Three boards. (1) The read board (scenes 2 to 4): coded base tiles in B4's `BasePiece` look; fragments as short tile rows; an assembly lane where overlaps snap together; a coded sequencing trace (a row of smooth peaks, each labelled with its base letter; at a heterozygous position two overlapping peaks with the label "A/T"); B9's `Pedigree` with a sequence chip under each symbol. (2) The gel board (scenes 5 to 8): a coded repeat strip (`RepeatStrip`: a marker drawn as a run of four-base blocks, each block labelled "GATA", with the count written at the end); a coded gel slab front-on (`Gel`: wells along the top edge labelled "wells", the top edge tagged "−, black lead", the bottom edge "+, red lead"; one lane per individual, headed with a pedigree symbol or a card; band positions computed from fragment length); the painted gel tank plate as context only. (3) The choice board (scenes 9, 12): two columns, "sequencing: base order" and "profiling: selected markers", filling with question cards. Individuals are always pedigree symbols (squares, circles) or coded cards, never people. Amber is the emphasis colour only. Electrode signs are written ("−", "+"), never colour only.
design.transitionPlan: The 1985 case and the band card open the lesson; the read board holds the two-tools split, the fragment lanes and the sickle family pedigree; the repeat strip carries short tandem repeats and hands over to the gel board for the gel, the child bands and the marker ladder; the choice board takes the tool choice and the limits; the memory aids and the decision rule follow; each attempt clears the board to one card (a paternity gel or a tool-choice question) and the feedback shrinks the card to a strip while the working writes on; scene crossfade with settle.
